name: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
title: Pattern 1: Draft, Then a Person Edits
answer: Draft, then a person edits is the simplest and most common pattern in this volume. An AI tool produces a first version of a document or plan, and a person reads it, corrects it, and decides whether it is used. Ownership rests with the person who signs the final version, so the AI acts more like a fast assistant than an author.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern solves the blank page problem. AI can start a lesson plan, a parent letter, practice questions, a rubric, a summary of an individualized education program for a parent, or a grant narrative. A person then fixes the draft and makes the final call about whether it goes out. The adult provides the judgment, and the tool provides speed. The pattern matters because the draft is never the finished product and responsibility stays with the person who signs the final version.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a preschool classroom, a teacher might ask an approved tool to draft the weekly note home and then add class news that only she knows. In a middle school, a science teacher might ask for three versions of the same reading at different levels and then check that the science stayed right in all three. In a high school, a counselor might draft a plain language explanation of graduation requirements for families. Across all these cases, the tool gets past the blank page and the adult provides the judgment. The text also notes that the pattern can apply to lesson plans, parent letters, practice questions, rubrics, IEP summaries for parents, and grant narratives.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text reports two studies. In one study, 15 teachers in five English primary schools used AI for lesson planning over two terms and reported that their weekly planning time fell from about 10 hours to under 5 (Carson et al., 2026). The same teachers said the saved time was often swallowed by other demands, so the hours never turned into anything a principal could see. In another study, researchers asked a chatbot to write a first grade science lesson, and the result was well organized and followed a familiar teaching model, but it included questionable steps, left out details, and listed a teaching resource that did not exist (Powell & Courchesne, 2024). The text says a teacher who skimmed it would have handed a fake source to a room full of six year olds, so the draft was useful only because a careful adult was going to read every line.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits. Drafts need real editing, not a quick glance, because the first grade science example shows that a draft can look organized while containing questionable steps, missing details, or a resource that does not exist. Figure 2.3 lays out four steps that make the pattern safe, and the level of checking increases when the stakes are higher. For anything touching a student's services, grades, or records, student names are removed before the text is entered, and the final version is compared with the actual file. That rule is simple to say but simple to overlook, so it appears in every chapter that uses this pattern. The decisions that stay with a person include reading, fixing, and deciding whether the draft goes out, and ownership stays with the person who signs the final version.
